# Diagnosing Clicking Noise in Automatic Transmission Engagement

A persistent, quiet clicking noise that appears exclusively when shifting into "Drive" or "Reverse," but vanishes immediately upon returning to "Neutral" or "Park," points directly to the torque converter clutch assembly or the transmission control module (TCM) logic rather than general drivetrain wear. In a 2003 Honda Accord equipped with the K24 engine and automatic transmission, this specific symptom pattern suggests an electrical or hydraulic engagement issue that only manifests under load conditions required for forward or reverse motion.

When you shift from Park to Drive without applying the brake pedal, many modern transmissions will hold the gear due to electronic safety interlocks designed to prevent unintended vehicle movement. However, the noise described indicates that the transmission is attempting to engage the torque converter clutch (TCC) prematurely. In this specific engine/transmission combination, the TCC lock-up solenoid may be receiving a premature signal from the TCM, or the solenoid itself could be stuck in a partial engagement state due to varnish buildup or internal failure.

The fact that the noise disappears in Neutral is critical. In Neutral, the input and output shafts are decoupled; the torque converter spins freely without driving the wheels. When you shift to Drive, the hydraulic pressure builds up, and the TCM commands the solenoid to lock the stator hub to the turbine housing. If that mechanical engagement happens while the engine RPM is fluctuating or if the slip between the clutch plates is uneven, it creates a rhythmic clicking sound similar to a failing starter motor or a loose alternator bearing.

To isolate the issue further, consider the condition of the transmission fluid. Over time, oxidation and heat can cause friction modifiers in the ATF (Automatic Transmission Fluid) to break down, creating a sludge that coats solenoid valves. This is particularly common in Honda transmissions from this era if the vehicle has seen high mileage without a flush. The resulting sticky solenoids fail to return to their "off" position cleanly when not commanded to lock up, causing chatter until the hydraulic pressure stabilizes.

Another potential culprit involves the shift interlock system or the brake pedal position sensor (BPS). While these usually prevent shifting out of Park entirely, a faulty BPS signal can confuse the TCM into thinking the vehicle is stationary when it isn't, leading to erratic solenoid behavior during the transition phase. If the car moves slightly before full engagement, the clutch packs may slip violently, generating the clicking noise heard in the video example.

Diagnostic steps should include checking for stored trouble codes in the OBD-II system, specifically looking for codes related to the TCM or TCC circuit. A multimeter test on the shift interlock solenoid can also reveal if it is drawing excessive current when engaged. If the electrical diagnostics return clean results, a transmission fluid and filter change using the correct specification (typically Honda ATF-Z1 or DW-1) might resolve sticky valves caused by degraded fluid chemistry.

It is worth noting that while this symptom often resolves with a fluid service, mechanical failure of the torque converter itself cannot be ruled out without removing the unit. However, given that driving performance remains normal with no clunks during gear changes, catastrophic internal damage is unlikely. The issue appears isolated to the engagement sequence rather than the operation of the gears themselves.

For those managing vehicle maintenance workflows or creating documentation for fleet diagnostics, recording audio and video samples before attempting repairs provides essential baseline data. This helps avoid misdiagnosis when a mechanic later replaces parts based on intermittent symptoms that may have resolved temporarily.
